cards.headline: Tapping buy is one decision. How you buy is another.
cards.body: Your broker gives you one box and several order types. Each one answers a single question: do you care more about getting filled, or about the price you pay? You cannot have both. Every order type is a different answer to that tradeoff.

cards.headline: A market order guarantees a fill, not a price.
cards.body: Send it and it executes almost immediately against whatever offers exist. That is the whole promise: you will be done. The number you end up paying is set by the order book at that instant, not by the quote you tapped.

cards.headline: A limit order guarantees a price, not a fill.
cards.body: Set a limit to buy at $20.00 and you will never pay $20.01. If the stock never trades down to $20.00, you simply do not own it. The order sits there while the price walks away. Price certainty, bought with execution uncertainty.

cards.prompt: A thinly traded company shows only 100 shares offered at $20.40. You send a market order for 500 shares. What are you actually promised?

options.label: All 500 fill, at prices you find out after

cards.explanation: The first 100 shares take the $20.40 offer. The other 400 climb the book — maybe $20.90, maybe $21.30. You are guaranteed to be **done**, not to like the average.

cards.headline: A stop order is a trigger, not a price.
cards.body: You own a stock at $52 and set a sell stop at $50. Nothing happens while it holds above. The moment $50 trades, your stop turns into a plain market order and sells at whatever price is available next.

cards.title: A stop through a gap down
cards.caption: Bad news overnight. The stock closes at $52.50 and opens at $44, straight past your $50 stop. The stop triggers at the open and fills near $44 — six dollars below your level.

cards.body: Once its trigger price trades, a plain stop order becomes a [[1]] order — so it fills at whatever the next available price happens to be.
cards.explanation: That is why a stop can get you out of a falling position, but never promises the price you get out at.

cards.headline: A stop-limit adds a floor, and a new risk.
cards.body: Stop at $50, limit at $48: you will never sell below $48. But if the stock gaps to $44 and keeps sliding, nothing fills. You still own it, all the way down. The floor that protected your price also trapped you.

cards.title: The four orders
cards.summary: Every order type trades one kind of certainty for another. Price or execution — decide which one matters more before you send it.
bullets: Market orders promise a fill and nothing about the price.
Limit orders promise a price and nothing about the fill.
A stop becomes a market order the instant it triggers.
A stop-limit defends your price and can leave you unfilled.

cards.insight: You can control the price you pay or the certainty of being filled. Never both. Every order you place is a choice between them.
